title: Longest Run of Consecutive Values
statement:
Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values: numbers x, x+1, x+2, … that all appear somewhere in the array.

The values can be anywhere in the array; their positions do not matter. Repeated values count once. Aim for O(n) time.

examples.why: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 are all present, scattered through the array. The other run, 2, 3, 4, has length 3.
The run is 7, 8, 9. Duplicates do not make it longer.

hints: Sorting solves it in O(n log n). To beat that, you need to ask "is x + 1 present?" in O(1). Which structure does that?
With a set you can count upward from any value. But counting from every value of a long run repeats the same work many times.
Only start counting from a value x when x − 1 is not in the set: x is then the first value of its run. Each value is then visited by at most one count.

explain.intuition:
Put every value in a set. Now a run can be walked by asking "is x + 1 here? and x + 2?". The waste comes from starting a walk in the middle of a run: from 12 you would recount 13 and 14, which the walk from 10 already counted.

So only start where a run begins, at values x with no x − 1 in the set. Every value is then stepped over by exactly one walk, and the total work is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop.
steps: Put all values into a set. This also removes duplicates.
For each value x in the set: if x − 1 is in the set, skip it, since it is not the start of a run.
Otherwise count upward: len = 1, and while x + len is in the set, len++.
Keep the largest len. Return it (0 for an empty array).
pitfalls: Looping over the original array instead of the set: with many duplicates of a run's first value, the same run is walked again for each copy, and the time becomes quadratic.
In the sorting approach, treating equal neighbours as a break in the run. In [7, 7, 8] the answer is 2, not 1.

solutions.title: Count up from every value
solutions.idea: Put values in a set and walk upward from each one. Correct, but a run of length L is recounted from each of its L values.

solutions.title: Sort and scan
solutions.idea: After sorting, a run is a stretch where each value is one more than the previous. Equal neighbours neither extend nor break it.

solutions.title: Set, counting only from run starts
solutions.idea: Walk upward only from values whose predecessor is missing. Each value is stepped over once in total.

followups: Return the run itself, not just its length.
Values arrive one at a time and you must report the longest run after each one. What structure merges runs as they touch?
